reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / AAO Basic and Clinical Science Course
clinicalPearls: A conical or spherical protrusion of the central anterior lens surface into the anterior chamber, arising from focal thinning and weakness of the anterior lens capsule
Bilateral anterior lenticonus is highly characteristic of Alport syndrome and should prompt evaluation for hereditary nephritis and sensorineural deafness

Retinoscopy classically shows an 'oil-droplet' central reflex with a scissoring or swirling reflex, and there is progressive axial myopia with irregular lenticular astigmatism not correctable by spectacles
Slit-lamp examination reveals a clear conical anterior bulge, best seen in retro-illumination, that increases the central lens power
Associated Alport features include anterior lens capsule fragility, a dot-and-fleck perimacular retinopathy, temporal retinal thinning and, occasionally, a posterior polymorphous-like corneal change
Spontaneous or minor-trauma rupture of the attenuated anterior capsule can occur, producing acute intumescent (swollen) lens changes
Distinguishing anterior lenticonus from keratoconus is essential, as both cause irregular astigmatism but the abnormality lies in the lens rather than the cornea

Definitive visual rehabilitation is by lens extraction with intraocular lens implantation once vision is significantly impaired, with attention to the abnormally thin and friable anterior capsule at surgery
reference.pathophysiology: The anterior lens capsule is a basement membrane composed largely of type IV collagen. In Alport syndrome, mutations in the genes encoding the alpha-3, alpha-4 or alpha-5 chains of type IV collagen (most commonly X-linked COL4A5, also autosomal COL4A3 and COL4A4) produce a structurally defective and abnormally thin anterior capsule. The weakened capsule can no longer resist the intralenticular pressure of the underlying cortex, so the central anterior surface progressively bulges forward into a cone. The resulting increase in central lens curvature causes lenticular myopia and irregular astigmatism, and the same collagen defect underlies the associated glomerular basement membrane disease and cochlear dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: Lens coloboma with focal shape abnormality
Anterior polar or pyramidal cataract distorting the reflex
Refractive lenticular myopia from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with retro-illumination to demonstrate the conical anterior bulge
Retinoscopy and refraction to detect the oil-droplet reflex and irregular lenticular astigmatism
Corneal topography and keratometry to exclude keratoconus as the source of astigmatism
Anterior segment imaging (Scheimpflug photography or anterior segment OCT) to characterise lens shape
Urinalysis and renal function testing for haematuria and nephropathy suggesting Alport syndrome
Pure-tone audiometry for sensorineural hearing loss
Genetic testing for type IV collagen (COL4A3/4/5) variants and screening of at-risk relatives
redFlags: Spontaneous or minor-trauma rupture of the thin anterior capsule with acute lens swelling and secondary pressure rise
Rapidly progressive myopic shift or fixed astigmatism unresponsive to spectacles in a child at amblyogenic age
Haematuria, proteinuria or declining renal function indicating progressive Alport nephropathy
reference.prognosis: Visual prognosis is generally good, with lens extraction and intraocular lens implantation restoring vision once the lenticular refractive error and any cataract are addressed. Overall prognosis is dominated by the associated Alport nephropathy, which may progress to end-stage renal disease requiring transplantation.
pitfalls: Attributing the irregular astigmatism to keratoconus and missing the lenticular origin
Failing to investigate for Alport syndrome when bilateral anterior lenticonus is found
Underestimating anterior capsule fragility, risking uncontrolled tears during capsulorhexis
Overlooking co-existing amblyopia in children by treating only the refractive error
Not screening family members for hereditary nephritis and hearing loss
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course (Lens and Cataract)
management: Restore vision by lens extraction with intraocular lens implantation once irregular lenticular myopia and astigmatism or cataract impair sight
Trial spectacle or contact lens correction, recognising it is often inadequate because of the irregular astigmatism
Refer for nephrological evaluation and management of the underlying Alport syndrome, including renin-angiotensin blockade to slow progression of nephropathy
Monitor renal function and manage progression towards end-stage renal disease with dialysis or transplantation
Assess hearing with audiology and provide hearing aids for sensorineural loss
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for X-linked or autosomal Alport syndrome
Coordinate multidisciplinary follow-up across ophthalmology, nephrology, audiology, and clinical genetics
